title: De lineis curvis non in eodem plano sitis, quae maximi minimive proprietate sunt praeditae

deep.reconstruction:
Problem IV of E740 asks for the space curve that makes \(\int \sqrt{(x^2+y^2+z^2)(dx^2+dy^2+dz^2)}\) extremal, i.e. \(\int r\,ds\) with \(r=|\mathbf r|\). This is a geodesic of the conformal metric \(r^2|d\mathbf r|^2\), or equivalently a ray of light in a medium with refractive index proportional to \(r\).

Set-up from the previous page: \(v=r\), \(s=\sqrt{1+p^2+q^2}\), \(p=dy/dx\), \(q=dz/dx\). Euler's three Euler–Lagrange relations are:
- (I) \(sx\,dx/v = d(v/s)\);
- (II) \(sy\,dx/v = d(vp/s)\);
- (III) \(sz\,dx/v = d(vq/s)\).

On this page (§24): expand \(d(vp/s) = v\,dp/s + p\,d(v/s)\) and use (I) for \(d(v/s)\). Relation (II) becomes \(s(y-px)\,dx/v = v\,dp/s\), i.e. \(y\,dx - x\,dy = v^2\,dp/s^2\). Likewise \(z\,dx - x\,dz = v^2\,dq/s^2\). In modern terms these are two components of the angular-momentum-type quantity \(\mathbf r \times (v/s)\,d\mathbf r/dx\), the conserved quantity that rotational symmetry (Noether) guarantees.

§25: dividing the two relations eliminates the factor \(v^2/s^2\), giving \(dp/(y-px) = dq/(z-qx)\). Since \(d(y-px) = -x\,dp\) and \(d(z-qx) = -x\,dq\), multiplying by \(-x\) makes both sides logarithmic differentials. Hence \(\ln(y-px) = \ln(z-qx) - \ln n\), so \(z-qx = n(y-px)\).

§26 (continued on the next page): substituting back into (II) gives \(dq = n\,dp\). So \(q = np + a\) and \(z = ny + ax + b\), with \(b=0\) forced by the previous relation. The extremal therefore lies in a plane through the centre.

The next page then separates the in-plane equation as \(-du/Q(u) = dp/Q(p)\). Geometrically, polar angle plus tangent angle is constant in the plane. The plane curves are the rectangular hyperbolas \(r^2\cos 2(\theta-\theta_0) = c\) centred at the origin, i.e. straight lines under \(w = z^2\).
errors: In §25 the printed step reads \(-x\,dp/(y-px) = x\,dq/(z-qx)\). Multiplying \(dp/(y-px) = dq/(z-qx)\) by \(-x\) should give a minus sign on both sides. As printed it would integrate to a product, not a ratio; the stated result \(z-qx = n(y-px)\) is nevertheless correct.
In §26 the print has \(\partial y = n\,\partial p\); it should be \(\partial q = n\,\partial p\). The next page (\(q = np + a\)) confirms that \(q\) is meant.

In §24 the expression for \(\partial.v/s\) appears printed with a stray minus under the fraction (\(sx\,\partial x/-v\)). By equation I it should be \(+sx\,\partial x/v\); the derived equations I and II are correct only with the plus sign.

ideas.what: Combining the Euler–Lagrange equations into the angular-momentum-type first integrals \(y\,dx - x\,dy = v^2\,dp/s^2\) and \(z\,dx - x\,dz = v^2\,dq/s^2\) for a rotationally symmetric functional.
ideas.modern_name: Conservation law from rotational symmetry (Noether's theorem; angular momentum for central problems)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Noether (1918) in general; for central forces Newton and Euler, and Laplace for the conserved angular momentum vector
ideas.where_published: Euler's mechanics of central forces (Mechanica, 1736) contains area/angular-momentum integrals; this page is the variational analogue

ideas.what: Extremals of \(\int f(r)\,ds\) in space are planar, lying in a plane through the centre.
ideas.modern_name: Planarity of geodesics of a spherically symmetric conformal metric / of light rays in a radially symmetric medium
ideas.usually_credited_to: Folklore; analogous to the planarity of central-force orbits
ideas.where_published: E740 itself (posthumous, 1813); possibly anticipated in other Euler isoperimetric papers

ideas.what: Integrating by noticing that the numerator is the differential of the denominator after multiplying by \(-x\), using \(d(y-px) = -x\,dp\).

deep.surprise_reason: The page carries out a correct, routine reduction showing that extremals of \(\int r\,ds\) are planar, via what amount to angular-momentum first integrals. This is natural and well known in substance (Noether, central forces). The only notable items are printing slips (sign error, \(\partial y\) for \(\partial q\)), not new mathematics.
transcription_corrections: The image shows \(-\frac{x\partial p}{y-px} = \frac{x\partial q}{z-qx}\), which matches the transcription. Mathematically the right side should carry a minus sign too.
'prodibitque \(\partial y = n\partial p\)' matches the print, but the intended statement is \(\partial q = n\partial p\).
\(\partial.\frac{v}{s} = \frac{sx\partial x}{-v}\): the apparent minus under the fraction is likely a print artifact; the correct value is \(+\frac{sx\partial x}{v}\).
